extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of medieval cathedral architecture, sculpture, and iconography; visitors to Amiens Cathedral
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting and 'reading' the sculptural program of a medieval cathedral façade (here Amiens): ordering of statues, iconographic symbolism, and didactic function so a spectator can understand the biblical and moral narrative encoded in the sculpture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Façade reading order
rubrics_metrics.description: The builder adopts a Scripture history on the façade so that it is to be read from left to right--i.e. from Christ's left to Christ's right, as He sees it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When approaching, read the sequence of statues and scenes in that direction; the arrangement of apostles, prophets, and minor prophets follows that left-to-right order and conveys the intended narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christ as central, cornerstone and organizing principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire mass of the front is seen, literally, as built on the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the chief corner-stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the façade as a theological structure: Christ central and primary, apostles and prophets as the foundational 'stone' and testimony; architectural features (receding porch, mid-pillar as 'Head of the Corner') physically express this idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and grouping of Apostles and Prophets
rubrics_metrics.description: Six apostles on Christ's right hand, and six on His left; four greater prophets on the sides of the porch; twelve minor prophets three to each of the four piers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spatial position (apse/curved bay vs. side piers) signals rank and role; know which named figure occupies each niche to read the program correctly (the text gives the precise order and names).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostles paired as opposite ranks expressing complementary virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The apostles stand in opposite ranks; under their feet in quatrefoil medallions are represented the virtues which each Apostle taught or manifested, arranged so left-hand virtues lead to right-hand complements (e.g., Courage to Faith; Patience to Hope; Gentillesse to Charity...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read each apostle together with the paired quatrefoil virtues (A and B) to understand the spiritual lesson; the left-right pairing is deliberate and pedagogical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statues and medallions as didactic 'Bible' to be read
rubrics_metrics.description: The series of sculpture in illustration of Apostolic and Prophetic teaching constitutes the 'Bible' of Amiens; lateral porches contain supplementary subjects necessary for pastoral and traditional teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the sculptural program as a textual/scriptural medium: scenes and symbols encode scriptural passages and moral instruction for the people of the day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quatrefoils are symbolic rather than representative
rubrics_metrics.description: All these quatrefoils are rather symbolic than representative; their purpose was answered enough if their sign was understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed naturalism was unnecessary for these medallions; clarity of sign (symbol) was the priority, and thus they were often entrusted to more inferior workmen than the principal sculptures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal prophetic/historical scenes executed by the ablest hands
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the subjects under the Prophets represent historical facts or real visions and have in general been executed by the ablest hands at the architect's command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect higher craftsmanship and more careful carving for major prophetic narratives; these reliefs are intended to be clearer, more animated, and more authoritative than decorative medallions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floral and vegetal pedestal symbolism for Christ
rubrics_metrics.description: On the pedestal are two flowers in vases (the lily on the north side and the rose on the south) and a tendril of vine on a minor stone, fulfilling the triple saying of Christ: 'I am the Rose of Sharon, and the Lily of the Valley.' 'I am the true Vine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify floral motifs (lily, rose, vine) as explicit references to Christ's self-descriptions; note that the sculpted lily is an idealized form (not fleur-de-lys) chosen for legibility and mode-of-growth symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporter and pedestal iconography (evil as subordinate instruments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporters—Cockatrice and Adder—represent the most active evil principles (infidelity of Pride and infidelity of Death) yet are still 'Pedestals of Christ' and in their deadly life accomplish His final will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read monstrous or evil creatures in pedestal/supportor positions as theological commentary: they symbolize vices or cosmic forces placed under Christ's dominion and used within the salvific order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beasts under Christ's feet denote distinct classes of sin
rubrics_metrics.description: Set under the feet of the statue of Christ are the lion and dragon; the images of Carnal sin, or Human sin, as distinguished from the Spiritual and Intellectual sin of Pride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different creatures symbolize different moral categories (e.g., lion and dragon = anger and lust; cockatrice = pride; adder = death/mud); use iconographic keys in the sculpture to read moral typologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture as symbol not idol: intended devotional signification
rubrics_metrics.description: No idol, in our sense of the word—only a letter, or sign of the Living Spirit—which was indeed conceived by every worshipper as here meeting him at the temple gate: the Word of Life, the King of Glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret figures as instructive signs pointing to spiritual realities; they function sacramentally/educationally rather than as objects of pagan idol worship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional iconographic cues (shields, attributes, posture, barefooting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shields bearing animals, objects (cup with cross for Faith), posture and accessories encode virtues and vices; e.g., barefoot = atheism/infidel, cup with cross = Faith, shield with lamb = gentillesse, shield with dove = humility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn conventional attributes to identify virtues/vices and roles: the text lists many local conventions (e.g., Perseverance often shown with lion, Chastity shield with Phoenix); these help decode otherwise stylized figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconographic distinction between idolatry and atheism
rubrics_metrics.description: Idolatry is faith in the wrong thing (kneeling to a monster), distinct from atheism (want of faith; e.g., the barefoot infidel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting bas-reliefs, note whether the scene criticizes belief in the wrong object (idolatry) or the absence of belief (atheism); the sculptors deliberately make that distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic convention: violent actions rendered feebly, quiet actions rendered well
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that all violent actions are in these bas-reliefs feebly or ludicrously expressed; quiet ones always right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect medieval sculptural style to favour composed, contemplative scenes over dramatic violence; this informs evaluation of workmanship and expressive intention in the reliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paired quatrefoil program beneath each statue (A and B; sometimes C and D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each principal statue has associated quatrefoils beneath it, marked upper (A) and lower (B) (angle prophets have four: A, B, C, D), illustrating either a virtue/vice pair or specific prophetic scenes with biblical citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To understand a statue's teaching, read its associated quatrefoils in sequence (A then B, etc.); the text gives a complete mapping (1–28) linking statue to its medallion subjects and scriptural references.
